items.title: Joe Wilder — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Franklin Hockster was his accompanist. I think that’s his name. He would accompany him on the piano, and he would play these solos.

ctx.x: How about in terms of tone? I’ve read a lot about people complimenting you on the tone that you get out of the instrument, and I heard it myself in the Smithsonian Jazz Orchestra.

When I was a kid coming up, that’s one of the things that was stressed to me by Mr. Griffin, who had a tremendous tone. He was a powerful cornet player. He played solos. In fact, when he – in Philadelphia, he and Josh Sadler, the violinist, was someone who was probably capable of making the Philadelphia Orchestra. But he’s the one that had the society band. They used to go down – he, and there was a pianist. The man’s name was Franklin Hockster, I think. He played concert music. When a station – I think it was…

That is one of those things that is very personal. The tone of an instrument is almost the personality of the person playing it. What other things run through your head when you’re improvising a solo? What kinds of things do you think about? Is it the tone and the . . . ?
